subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Mood disorder spectrum and bipolar I vs II
vignette: A 34-year-old woman describes episodes lasting weeks at a time when she feels on top of the world, needs little sleep, and spends compulsively, alternating with periods of profound sadness and hopelessness. Between episodes she functions at her baseline. These swings have strained her relationships and led to the loss of two jobs. She reports no fixed false beliefs or hallucinations.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the class of illness represented by this patient's symptoms?

options.text: An abnormal range of moods or emotional states with loss of control, causing distress and impairment in social or occupational functioning
Fixed, false, idiosyncratic beliefs that persist despite evidence to the contrary
Perceptions in the absence of external stimuli, most often auditory
A gradual, progressive decline in memory and cognition with preserved mood
Transient symptoms that begin and end within hours of an identifiable stressor

explanation_correct: Mood disorders are characterized by an abnormal range of moods or internal emotional states together with a loss of control over them. The severity of the mood disturbance causes distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning, as in this patient. The category includes major depressive, bipolar, dysthymic, and cyclothymic disorders. Her alternating elevated and depressive episodes with clear functional impairment fit a bipolar spectrum mood disorder.

explanation_incorrect.B: Fixed false beliefs that persist despite contrary evidence define delusions, a psychotic symptom rather than the defining feature of a mood disorder.
explanation_incorrect.C: Perceptions in the absence of external stimuli are hallucinations; they can accompany mood episodes but do not define a mood disorder.
explanation_incorrect.D: Progressive memory and cognitive decline with relatively preserved mood suggests a neurocognitive disorder such as dementia, not a primary mood disorder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Symptoms beginning and ending within hours of a stressor are more consistent with an adjustment or acute stress reaction, not the sustained episodes described here.

educationalObjective: Mood disorders involve an abnormal range of moods with loss of control, producing distress and functional impairment; they include major depressive, bipolar, dysthymic, and cyclothymic disorders.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Mood disorder spectrum and bipolar I vs II
vignette: A 28-year-old man has a history of several 10-day periods of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and reckless spending that resulted in substantial financial losses and the loss of his job. He has also had two separate 3-month periods of depressed mood, anhedonia, and fatigue. He has never had hallucinations or delusions and has never been hospitalized.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar II disorder, because he has had both hypomanic and depressive episodes
Cyclothymic disorder, because his symptoms alternate over years
Bipolar I disorder, because a full manic episode has occurred
Major depressive disorder, because depressive episodes predominate
Schizoaffective disorder, because psychotic symptoms accompany mood changes

explanation_correct: Bipolar I disorder requires at least one manic episode; hypomanic or depressive episodes may also occur and may be separated by any length of time. His 10-day episodes of elevated mood with decreased sleep, pressured speech, and reckless spending causing job loss and financial harm meet criteria for mania because they lasted at least 1 week and caused marked impairment. The diagnosis is therefore bipolar I, even though he has never had psychosis or required hospitalization.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bipolar II requires a hypomanic episode and a major depressive episode but no history of mania; his episodes caused marked impairment and lasted 10 days, making them manic.
explanation_incorrect.B: Cyclothymic disorder involves at least 2 years of mild fluctuating hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet full episode criteria; his episodes are full-blown.
explanation_incorrect.D: Major depressive disorder is excluded by a history of mania; the presence of a manic episode mandates a bipolar spectrum diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychotic symptoms for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a mood episode; he has no psychotic symptoms at all.

educationalObjective: A single full manic episode establishes bipolar I disorder regardless of the presence or absence of psychotic features, hospitalization, or depressive episodes.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Mood disorder spectrum and bipolar I vs II
vignette: A 41-year-old woman has a long-standing mood disorder. During one episode she believed her coworkers were plotting to poison her and reported hearing voices commenting on her actions; these symptoms resolved fully as her mood returned to baseline. During a later, milder 5-day period of elevated mood and increased energy she felt unusually productive but had no unusual beliefs or perceptions and continued working normally.
question: Which of the following statements about psychotic features in mood disorders is most accurate?

options.text: Psychotic features can occur during hypomanic episodes but not during manic or depressive episodes
Psychotic features may occur during manic or major depressive episodes but not during hypomanic episodes
The presence of hallucinations or delusions automatically establishes a diagnosis of schizophrenia
Psychotic symptoms that resolve with mood normalization indicate schizoaffective disorder
Mood disorders with psychotic features require psychotic symptoms to persist at least 2 weeks without a mood episode

explanation_correct: In mood disorders, episodic psychotic features — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or behavior — may be present at any time during a mood episode, but this applies to manic and major depressive episodes and not to hypomania. Hypomania by definition lacks psychotic features and does not cause marked impairment. Her psychotic symptoms occurred only during a full mood episode and remitted with it, consistent with a mood disorder with psychotic features.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hypomania specifically excludes psychotic features; it is the manic and depressive episodes that may carry them.
explanation_incorrect.C: Psychosis can be secondary to mood disorders, medical illness, or substances; psychosis alone does not establish schizophrenia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a mood episode; here psychosis remitted with mood and never occurred alone.
explanation_incorrect.E: That 2-week psychosis-alone requirement is the criterion for schizoaffective disorder, not for a mood disorder with psychotic features.

educationalObjective: Psychotic features may accompany manic and major depressive episodes but never hypomania; psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Mood disorder spectrum and bipolar I vs II
vignette: A 33-year-old man presents with 6 weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, and suicidal ideation, accompanied by auditory hallucinations telling him he is being punished for his sins. The hallucinations began 1 week after the mood symptoms and disappear entirely when his depression is treated. One month later he has a 2-week period in which he hears the voices again while his mood is completely normal.
question: Which of the following best explains the diagnostic significance of the 2-week period of psychosis during euthymia?

options.text: It confirms major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features, which permits psychosis between episodes
It is consistent with bipolar II disorder, in which psychotic features accompany hypomania
It rules out any mood disorder because psychosis can never occur in unipolar depression
It establishes schizoaffective disorder, because psychotic symptoms occurred for at least 2 weeks without a mood episode
It indicates brief psychotic disorder, because the psychosis was stress related and lasted less than 1 month

explanation_correct: Schizoaffective disorder shares symptoms with both schizophrenia and mood disorders, but it is distinguished from a mood disorder with psychotic features by the requirement that psychotic symptoms occur for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a manic or depressive episode. This patient's 2-week period of auditory hallucinations while euthymic meets that criterion, so schizoaffective disorder is the appropriate diagnosis. By contrast, psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features.

explanation_incorrect.A: In a mood disorder with psychotic features, psychotic symptoms occur only within mood episodes; persistent psychosis during euthymia argues against it.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bipolar II disorder involves hypomania and major depression, and psychotic features do not occur during hypomania; this man has no hypomanic episode.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mood disorders can include psychotic features during manic or depressive episodes, so psychosis does not exclude a mood disorder — but it does change the diagnosis here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Brief psychotic disorder is a short, stress-related psychosis lasting 1 day to 1 month, but when psychosis persists at least 2 weeks during euthymia in a mood-disordered patient, schizoaffective disorder takes precedence.

educationalObjective: Psychosis lasting at least 2 weeks in the absence of a mood episode distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from a mood disorder with psychotic features.
